---
title: "Aggregate-Level Covariate-Distance Matching"
---

## Introduction {#sec-distance-intro}

Consider a situation that arises constantly in oncology health technology assessment (HTA). A novel
therapy, say a CAR-T cell product for relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma, is licensed on the
strength of a **single-arm** Phase II trial: every enrolled patient received the new agent, so the trial
carries no internal control against which a treatment effect could be measured. To report how the new
agent compares with standard chemoimmunotherapy, the analyst must borrow a control arm from *outside* the
trial, from one of several external Phase III trials or disease registries of the standard regimens. Those
external studies do not contain the new agent, so there is no shared treatment to anchor the comparison,
and they rarely release patient-level data; each publishes only a short table of baseline covariate means,
mean age, proportion male, a mean severity marker, and little else. Which external study should supply the
borrowed control arm? Choosing wrongly can reverse the sign of the reported effect and drive a
reimbursement decision the wrong way, so the stakes are the whole submission. This chapter answers the
prior question that every method of Parts IV and V silently assumed away: *before* adjusting for
population differences, how do we choose the comparator study to adjust toward, using only the aggregate
covariate summaries the external studies report? The workable answer, together with a sharp statement of
what it can and cannot guarantee, is the subject of the chapter, and we will follow one running trial
example (@exm-distance-two-trials) from the first definition to the final caveat.

Every method in Parts IV and V began once a comparator had already been chosen. Matching-adjusted
indirect comparison (Chapter 18), simulated treatment comparison (Chapter 19), multilevel network
meta-regression (Chapter 20), and multilevel unanchored meta-regression (Chapter 26) all take as given a
pair of studies, an index trial with individual patient data (IPD) and a designated comparator trial with
aggregate data (AgD), and then do the work of bridging their populations. In a connected anchored network
the comparator is not a choice at all: the common control treatment forces it, and the only question is
how to adjust. But two situations strip away that luxury. A **disconnected network** offers several AgD
studies, none sharing a common comparator with the index trial, any of which could in principle serve as
the external arm for an unanchored comparison; the analyst must select one. A **single-arm study**, having
no internal control, must borrow its entire comparator arm from an external population, and the choice of
which external study to borrow is the whole analysis. This chapter is about that prior choice: how to pick
a comparator study before the population-adjustment machinery is switched on.

The practical rule, described in a Bristol Compass blog post on disconnected ML-NMR [@perren2024compass]
and implemented in the `uitc` R package [@uitc], is disarmingly simple. Each candidate comparator study reports a vector of
covariate summaries, typically baseline means; the index population reports its own; choose the candidate
whose summaries lie **closest** to the index population on some distance between summary vectors. The
content of the rule is entirely in the word "closest," because there is no single distance on
$\mathbb{R}^p$ and the candidates can be ranked differently by different choices. We develop the natural
candidates: the Euclidean and standardized Euclidean distances (@def-euclidean-distance), the Mahalanobis
distance and its identification with a whitened Euclidean distance (@thm-mahalanobis-whitening), and the
Manhattan, Minkowski, Gower, and mean-absolute standardized-mean-difference distances
(@def-distance-variants). We prove which of these are invariant to a change in the units of a covariate
and which are not (@thm-distance-scale-invariance, @prp-distance-scale-dependence), because a distance
whose ranking flips when age is recorded in months rather than years is a poor basis for a decision.

We then ask the only question that matters for validity: does a small covariate-summary distance bound the
**bias** of the eventual adjusted estimate? The answer is a sharp dichotomy that this chapter proves in
full. When the conditional contrast is affine in the covariates, the transport bias is *exactly* a linear
functional of the covariate-mean gap, and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality turns any of the quadratic-form
distances into a rigorous bias bound (@thm-distance-linear-bias-bound), connecting comparator selection
directly to the unanchored consistency theorem of Chapter 17 (@thm-unanchored-paic-consistency). When the
contrast is merely Lipschitz, a bias bound survives, but only against the **Wasserstein distance between
full distributions** (@thm-lipschitz-bias-bound), and a distance between *means* is provably not a
Wasserstein distance: it is a lower bound on it, never an upper bound. The consequence, made precise in
@prp-distance-diagnostic-not-validity, is the central honest caveat of the chapter. Two populations can
have identical covariate means, hence zero distance under every metric we define, and yet different target
effects, because a nonlinear contrast sees the spread and not only the center, and because an unmeasured
prognostic variable can differ while every observed summary agrees. Aggregate-level distance matching is
therefore a **diagnostic and design tool**, not a transportability theorem: a small distance makes a
population bridge more plausible and, under linearity, controls the residual bias, but it certifies
neither the shared prognostic factor assumption (@def-spfa) nor conditional constancy of absolute effects
(@def-conditional-constancy-absolute) nor the absence of unmeasured imbalance. A fully worked example
ranking four candidate comparators under five criteria, in which the three principal distances each select
a different winner and the actual bias is computed exactly, closes the development. This material is an
extension beyond the population-adjustment theory of @phillippo2019thesis, prompted by the
disconnected-network setting of @chandler2025mlumr, and corresponds to results O.1 to O.7 of the proof
catalogue.

Throughout, $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0\in\mathbb{R}^p$ denotes the covariate-summary vector of the **index**
population (the population in which we hold IPD, or whose effect we wish to report), and
$\bar{\mathbf{x}}_1,\dots,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_J\in\mathbb{R}^p$ the summary vectors of the $J$ candidate
comparator studies, following the study-mean notation $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j$ of [Notation](/notation.qmd).
We write $\boldsymbol{\delta}_j=\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0$ for the **covariate gap** of
candidate $j$, $\ell\in\{1,\dots,p\}$ for the covariate index, and $\|\mathbf{v}\|_A=\sqrt{\mathbf{v}^\top
A\,\mathbf{v}}$ for the quadratic-form norm of a positive-definite $A$. The bold vector
$\boldsymbol{\delta}_j$, a gap between covariate means, is a different object from the plain scalar
$\delta_{j,\,t_1 t_k}$ of [Notation](/notation.qmd), which is a within-study treatment contrast; the
boldface marks the vector throughout, following the vector-versus-scalar convention of the book, and the
two never appear together. Read $\|\mathbf{v}\|_A$ simply as "the length of $\mathbf{v}$ measured with the
ruler $A$": when $A=I$ it is the ordinary length, and a general $A\succ0$ (read $A\succ0$ as "$A$ is
symmetric positive definite," so that $\mathbf{v}^\top A\mathbf{v}>0$ for every $\mathbf{v}\ne\mathbf 0$
and the square root is real) stretches some directions and shrinks others.

A reader who wants the destination before the journey can consult the map in @tbl-distance-roadmap. The
single practical recommendation, defended in the sections that follow, is compressed into it: if you
compute only one distance, compute the **standardized Euclidean distance**, and if the index study
supplies a covariance matrix, add the **Mahalanobis distance** and treat any disagreement between the two
as a signal that the ranking depends on covariate correlations rather than on the data.

| Distance | What the number captures | Units-safe? | Defined in |
|---|---|:--:|---|
| Raw Euclidean $d_E$ | straight-line gap in the recorded units | no | @def-euclidean-distance |
| Standardized Euclidean $d_{SE}$ (default) | gap in standard-deviation units, one per covariate | yes | @def-euclidean-distance |
| Mahalanobis $d_M$ | gap measured against the index covariate correlation cloud | yes | @def-mahalanobis-distance |
| Manhattan, Minkowski, Chebyshev $d_q$ | sum, blend, or single worst standardized gap | yes | @def-distance-variants |
| Mean-SMD $d_{\mathrm{SMD}}$ | average standardized gap; ties to balance tables | yes | @def-distance-variants |
| Gower $d_G$ | mixed continuous and binary covariates on one scale | yes | @def-distance-variants |

: Roadmap of the covariate-summary distances of this chapter. "Units-safe" means the ranking of candidates does not change when a covariate is re-expressed in different units (@thm-distance-scale-invariance, @prp-distance-scale-dependence). Every distance here is a diagnostic of population similarity, never by itself a proof that the eventual comparison is unbiased (@prp-distance-diagnostic-not-validity). {#tbl-distance-roadmap}

## The comparator-selection problem {#sec-distance-problem}

We fix the decision the chapter addresses.

::: {#def-comparator-selection}
## Aggregate-level comparator selection
Let the index population have covariate-summary vector $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0\in\mathbb{R}^p$, and let
candidate comparator studies $j=1,\dots,J$ report covariate-summary vectors
$\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j\in\mathbb{R}^p$ on the same $p$ covariates. Given a distance
$d:\mathbb{R}^p\times\mathbb{R}^p\to[0,\infty)$ on summary vectors, the **aggregate-level matching rule**
selects
$$
j^{*}\;\in\;\arg\min_{1\le j\le J}\; d\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j\big).
$$ {#eq-distance-argmin}
The selected study $j^{*}$ is the observed comparator whose reported population summaries are closest to
the index population on the chosen scale. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** Each candidate study is reduced to one number, its distance from the index
population, and the rule picks the smallest. The only content is what "distance" means, because a candidate
that looks closest under one sensible distance can look farthest under another. The rest of the chapter is
a tour of the reasonable choices and a proof of exactly how much a small distance does, and does not, buy
you. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

We anchor every definition to one small scenario, carried from here to the end of the chapter.

::: {#exm-distance-two-trials}
## A running example: two candidate comparator trials
Return to the single-arm lymphoma trial of the introduction. The **index** study reports two baseline
covariate means, mean age in years and a mean severity biomarker in its natural units, and two external
Phase III trials, $P$ and $Q$, are candidate sources of the borrowed control arm. Their reported means
are

| Covariate ($\ell$) | reference scale $s_\ell$ | index mean $\bar{x}_{0\ell}$ | Study $P$ mean | Study $Q$ mean |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| age (years) | $10$ | $60$ | $70$ | $66$ |
| biomarker (units) | $4$ | $10$ | $14$ | $6$ |

The reference scales $s=(10,4)$ are the index-study standard deviations of the two covariates. The index
covariance, also from the index study, is
$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{pmatrix}100 & 20\\ 20 & 16\end{pmatrix},
$$
so age and biomarker are positively correlated, $\operatorname{corr}=20/(10\cdot4)=0.5$. The covariate
gaps and their standardized versions $\mathbf{z}_j=(\delta_{j1}/s_1,\ \delta_{j2}/s_2)$ are
$$
\boldsymbol{\delta}_P=(10,\ 4),\quad \mathbf{z}_P=(1.0,\ 1.0);
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\delta}_Q=(6,\ -4),\quad \mathbf{z}_Q=(0.6,\ -1.0).
$$
In words: Study $P$'s patients are older **and** have a higher biomarker, both covariates up together, the
direction in which age and biomarker naturally co-vary in the index trial. Study $Q$'s patients are
somewhat older but have a **lower** biomarker, the two covariates moving in opposite directions, against
the correlation. The central surprise of the chapter, foreshadowed here and computed in
@sec-distance-euclidean and @sec-distance-mahalanobis, is that raw and standardized Euclidean distance
will both judge $Q$ the closer match, while the Mahalanobis distance will judge $P$ the closer match,
purely because $P$ respects the age-biomarker correlation and $Q$ fights it. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The rule @eq-distance-argmin is a *design rule*: it ranks the candidates and names a winner, to be fed
into an unanchored MAIC, STC, or ML-UMR. It is not yet a claim about validity. To see both what it can do
and what it cannot, recall the two regimes that make it necessary.

::: {.remark}
**Why selection is forced in disconnected and single-arm evidence.** In the anchored triangle of
Chapter 14 the index trial $AC$ and the comparator trial $BC$ share the control $C$, and the Bucher
contrast $\hat d_{AB}=\hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC}$ differences the shared anchor away. A **disconnected**
network has no such shared treatment between the index trial and the studies reporting the comparator of
interest, so there is no anchor to difference and the comparison must be **unanchored**: the absolute
outcome of the index treatment is compared to the absolute outcome of a comparator drawn from a *different*
population (Chapter 17, @thm-unanchored-paic-consistency; Chapter 26). When several AgD studies report that
comparator, each defines a different bridging population, and the analyst must choose. A **single-arm**
index study is the limiting case: lacking any internal control, its entire counterfactual arm is an
external population, and selecting the most similar external study is the only lever available. In both
regimes the choice precedes, and conditions the credibility of, the adjustment that follows. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What a good choice buys, and what it does not.** Unanchored population adjustment is consistent only
when every imbalanced prognostic variable and effect modifier is measured and balanced and the target
covariate values lie inside the index covariate support (@thm-unanchored-paic-consistency, hypotheses
(iii) and (iv)). Choosing a comparator with smaller covariate gaps makes both conditions easier to meet: a
smaller gap typically means less reweighting, a higher effective sample size (@thm-maic-ess-bound), and a target
nearer the interior of the support, so finite stable weights are more likely to exist. The distance is a
proxy for "how hard the bridge will be." It is not a proxy for "whether the bridge is valid," because the
unmeasured and the nonlinear escape it entirely; that gap is the subject of @sec-distance-caveat. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This setup corresponds to O.1 in the proof catalogue.

## A practical workflow, and what selection is for {#sec-distance-workflow}

Before any algebra, it helps to see where comparator selection sits in a real submission. Distance
matching is one step of a longer pipeline, and it is neither the first step nor the last.

1. **Fix the target.** State the population in which the effect must be reported (here, the index
single-arm trial's population) and the estimand (for instance, a marginal log odds ratio versus standard
of care). Everything downstream is measured against this target.
2. **Assemble candidates.** From a systematic review, list every external study that reports the
comparator treatment *and* the baseline covariates you will need. These are the candidate comparators
$j=1,\dots,J$.
3. **Screen for clinical and design comparability first.** Before computing a single distance, discard
candidates that differ in line of therapy, outcome definition, follow-up length, standard of care,
eligibility, or measurement practice. Distance matching operates only among studies that already pass
this clinical screen; a small covariate distance cannot rescue an incomparable trial.
4. **Choose the covariate set.** Include the effect modifiers and prognostic variables that are both
clinically justified and reported across the surviving candidates, and record which important covariates
are missing from which studies.
5. **Harmonize and scale.** Put every covariate on a common definition, choose reference scales, and
compute several distances. Inspect which covariates drive each distance and estimate the effective sample
size (ESS) the eventual reweighting would leave (@sec-distance-bias, @thm-maic-ess-bound).
6. **Carry uncertainty forward.** Feed the chosen comparator into an unanchored MAIC, STC, or ML-UMR, and
carry any disagreement between distances, any missing covariate, and any residual imbalance into a
quantitative bias analysis (Chapter 28).

| Step | Question it answers | Tool |
|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 target | For whom must the effect hold? | estimand definition (Chapter 12, Chapter 17) |
| 2 candidates | Which external studies could supply the arm? | systematic review |
| 3 clinical screen | Are the trials comparable at all? | clinical and design appraisal |
| 4 covariates | Which variables enter the gap? | effect-modifier and prognosis judgment |
| 5 distance and ESS | Which candidate is closest, and how costly? | this chapter, @thm-maic-ess-bound |
| 6 sensitivity | What could still go wrong? | quantitative bias analysis (Chapter 28) |

: The place of aggregate-level distance matching (steps 4 and 5) in a comparator-selection workflow. {#tbl-distance-workflow}

::: {.remark}
**Why a cheap pre-analysis screen, rather than adjusting on every candidate.** A natural objection is: if
there are four candidate comparators, why not simply run four unanchored MAICs and keep the one with the
best effective sample size? Three reasons. First, an unanchored adjustment against a badly matched
comparator can produce extreme weights, a tiny ESS, or an optimization that fails to converge at all, so
the "try them all" strategy often has no clean output to compare. Second, choosing the comparator *after*
seeing four different treatment estimates is selection on the outcome: it inflates the apparent effect and
destroys any pre-registration guarantee. Third, distance matching is computed from published covariate
tables alone, before the outcome is touched, so it is cheap, reproducible, and blind to the answer. It is
a screen, run once, up front, on data an HTA reviewer can check. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Where entropy balancing and individual-level reweighting live.** The word "matching" in this chapter's
title is aggregate-level: it matches *summary vectors*, not patients. The individual-level reweighting
tools, the method-of-moments weights of MAIC (Chapter 18), and entropy balancing (Hainmueller's minimum
relative-entropy weights, derived in the individual-level setting), operate *after* a comparator has been
chosen and require the index individual patient data; they solve a different problem, how to reweight
patients so that a chosen comparator's moments are met. This chapter is strictly the upstream, aggregate
step that decides *which* comparator to reweight toward, using only the means each study publishes. If you
were expecting entropy balancing here, it belongs to the individual-level material of Chapter 18; distance
matching is the design step before it. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Choosing the covariates and the reference scales.** Two applied choices decide what the distance
measures.

- *Which covariates.* Include a covariate only if it is a plausible effect modifier (@def-effect-modifier)
or prognostic variable (@def-prognostic-variable) *and* is reported by every surviving candidate. A
covariate reported by some candidates but not others cannot enter a common distance; dropping a genuine
effect modifier to keep a candidate in the running is a substantive decision to be recorded, not hidden.
Do not pad the distance with many weakly prognostic covariates: each one dilutes the gaps that actually
drive bias.
- *Which reference scale.* When the index individual patient data are available, the index standard
deviations are the natural reference scales, because the eventual reweighting is toward the index
population. When no IPD are available, a pooled or comparator-reported standard deviation is used instead;
for a binary covariate with prevalence $\pi$, the Bernoulli standard deviation $\sqrt{\pi(1-\pi)}$ is
standard; a missing standard deviation is usually borrowed from a comparable covariate or a pooled value.
Note the asymmetry proved later: re-expressing a covariate in different **units** does not change the
standardized ranking (@thm-distance-scale-invariance), but changing the **reference scale** while holding
units fixed can change the winner (@exr-distance-rescale-ranking), so the reference-scale choice is a
modeling decision that belongs in the write-up, not a harmless re-expression. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Euclidean and standardized Euclidean distances {#sec-distance-euclidean}

The first candidate is the ordinary straight-line distance, and its first defect is that it depends on the
units in which the covariates happen to be recorded.

::: {#def-euclidean-distance}
## Euclidean and standardized Euclidean distance
The **Euclidean distance** between the index summary $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0$ and a candidate summary
$\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j$ is the $\ell_2$ norm of their gap,
$$
d_E\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j\big)\;=\;\big\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big\|_2
\;=\;\sqrt{\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}\big(\bar{x}_{j\ell}-\bar{x}_{0\ell}\big)^2}.
$$ {#eq-distance-euclidean}
Let $s_1,\dots,s_p>0$ be **reference scales**, one per covariate, typically an IPD standard deviation, a
reported comparator standard deviation, or, for a binary covariate with prevalence $\pi$, the Bernoulli
standard deviation $\sqrt{\pi(1-\pi)}$. Writing $S=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\dots,s_p)$ and the
**standardized gap** $\mathbf{z}_j=S^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j$, with components
$z_{j\ell}=(\bar{x}_{j\ell}-\bar{x}_{0\ell})/s_\ell$, the **standardized Euclidean distance** is
$$
d_{SE}\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;s\big)\;=\;\big\|\mathbf{z}_j\big\|_2
\;=\;\big\|S^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big\|_2
\;=\;\sqrt{\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}\left(\frac{\bar{x}_{j\ell}-\bar{x}_{0\ell}}{s_\ell}\right)^2}.
$$ {#eq-distance-stdeuclidean}
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why standardize.** The raw distance @eq-distance-euclidean adds squared gaps measured in incompatible
units, so it is dominated by whichever covariate carries the largest numerical magnitude. A gap of one
year in mean age and a gap of $0.5$ in a proportion contribute $1$ and $0.25$ to the raw squared distance,
yet the proportion gap is a far larger fraction of that covariate's natural spread. Dividing each gap by a
reference scale renders the contributions commensurate: each standardized component $z_{j\ell}$ is the
familiar **standardized mean difference** of that covariate, a dimensionless number measured in standard
deviations. The `uitc` package defaults to $d_{SE}$ for exactly this reason, reserving the raw $d_E$ for
covariates that are already on a common scale. The formal statement that standardization removes the unit
dependence is @thm-distance-scale-invariance below. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The running example, raw and standardized.** Take the two candidate trials of @exm-distance-two-trials.
The raw Euclidean distances are
$$
d_E(P)=\sqrt{10^2+4^2}=\sqrt{116}=10.77,
\qquad
d_E(Q)=\sqrt{6^2+(-4)^2}=\sqrt{52}=7.21,
$$
and the standardized Euclidean distances, using the standardized gaps $\mathbf{z}_P=(1.0,1.0)$ and
$\mathbf{z}_Q=(0.6,-1.0)$, are
$$
d_{SE}(P)=\sqrt{1.0^2+1.0^2}=\sqrt2=1.414,
\qquad
d_{SE}(Q)=\sqrt{0.6^2+1.0^2}=\sqrt{1.36}=1.166 .
$$
The standardized numbers read directly as "how many standard deviations apart": Study $P$ is exactly one
standard deviation older and one higher on the biomarker; Study $Q$ is $0.6$ standard deviations older and
one lower. Both the raw and the standardized distance rank $Q$ ahead of $P$. Hold on to that ranking:
@sec-distance-mahalanobis overturns it once the age-biomarker correlation is taken into account.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This material corresponds to O.2 in the proof catalogue.

## The Mahalanobis distance and whitening {#sec-distance-mahalanobis}

Standardization rescales each covariate but ignores their correlations. When the index IPD supplies a full
covariance matrix, the Mahalanobis distance uses it, and the use turns out to be exactly a change of
coordinates that decorrelates and standardizes the covariates simultaneously, an operation called
**whitening** (the name borrows from signal processing: it turns a correlated covariate cloud into an
uncorrelated, unit-variance cloud, like the flat spectrum of white noise). Before any formula, here is the
picture to carry: the Mahalanobis distance asks whether the *whole pattern* of covariate differences looks
unusual relative to the index trial's covariate cloud. A gap that points along a direction in which the
index patients naturally vary, or in which two covariates move together as they usually do, is
unremarkable and counts for little; the same-sized gap in a direction the index patients rarely move, or
against a correlation they usually respect, is surprising and counts for a lot.

::: {#def-mahalanobis-distance}
## Mahalanobis distance
Let $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$ be a positive-definite covariance matrix for the
covariates, typically the index-IPD sample covariance. The **Mahalanobis distance** is the
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$-quadratic-form norm of the gap,
$$
d_M\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\big)
\;=\;\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\delta}_j^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j}
\;=\;\big\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}}.
$$ {#eq-distance-mahalanobis}
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** The Mahalanobis distance is the quadratic-form norm
$\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}}$ from the chapter opening: the length of the gap
measured with the ruler $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$ in place of the identity (recall $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
\succ0$ means $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is symmetric positive definite, so $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$ exists and
the square root is real). The ruler $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$ is large in directions where the index
patients are tightly clustered and small in directions where they are widely spread, so it charges a heavy
price for a gap along a low-variance direction and a light price for a gap along a high-variance one. When
the covariates are uncorrelated and on equal footing, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=I$, the ruler is the identity
and $d_M$ is the ordinary Euclidean distance. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The defining identity is that this distance is an ordinary Euclidean distance after a linear transform
that "whitens" the covariates, that is, makes their covariance the identity. We prove it for any matrix
square root, then specialize to the two used in practice.

::: {#thm-mahalanobis-whitening}
## Whitening equivalence of the Mahalanobis distance
Let $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ 0$ and let $B\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$ be any invertible matrix with
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=BB^\top$ (such a $B$ exists by @thm-cov-psd). Then the Mahalanobis distance is the
Euclidean norm of the **whitened gap** $B^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j$:
$$
d_M\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\big)
\;=\;\big\|B^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big\|_2 .
$$ {#eq-distance-whitening}
In particular this holds for the lower-triangular Cholesky factor $B=L$ with
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=LL^\top$, and for the symmetric positive-definite square root
$B=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}$ of @thm-cov-psd. Moreover:

1. If $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\operatorname{diag}(s_1^2,\dots,s_p^2)$ is diagonal, then $d_M$ reduces to the
standardized Euclidean distance $d_{SE}$ with reference scales $s_\ell$.

2. If $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is the covariance of the covariate vector $\mathbf{X}$, the whitened vector
$B^{-1}\mathbf{X}$ has identity covariance: $\operatorname{Cov}(B^{-1}\mathbf{X})=
B^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}B^{-\top}=I_p$.
:::

::: {.proof}
That a factorization $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=BB^\top$ with invertible $B$ exists is part of @thm-cov-psd:
since $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ0$ is symmetric, the spectral theorem writes $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=Q\Lambda
Q^\top$ with $Q$ orthogonal ($Q^\top Q=I$) and $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_p)$,
and positive-definiteness forces every eigenvalue $\lambda_i>0$; the spectral
construction there produces the symmetric square root $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}=Q\operatorname{diag}
(\sqrt{\lambda_1},\dots,\sqrt{\lambda_p})Q^\top$, which is invertible because every $\lambda_i>0$ and
satisfies $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$; taking
$B=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}$ (symmetric, so $B=B^\top$ and $BB^\top=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$) gives one such
$B$, and the Cholesky factor gives another.

For any invertible $B$ with $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=BB^\top$, taking inverses and using
$(BB^\top)^{-1}=B^{-\top}B^{-1}$,
$$
\boldsymbol{\delta}_j^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j
=\boldsymbol{\delta}_j^\top B^{-\top}B^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j
=\big(B^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big)^\top\big(B^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big)
=\big\|B^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big\|_2^2 .
$$
Taking nonnegative square roots gives @eq-distance-whitening. For part 1, if
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\operatorname{diag}(s_1^2,\dots,s_p^2)$ then
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(s_1^{-2},\dots,s_p^{-2})$ and
$$
\boldsymbol{\delta}_j^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j
=\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}\frac{\delta_{j\ell}^2}{s_\ell^2}
=\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}\left(\frac{\bar{x}_{j\ell}-\bar{x}_{0\ell}}{s_\ell}\right)^2
=d_{SE}\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;s\big)^2 ,
$$
which is @eq-distance-stdeuclidean. For part 2, the covariance of a linear map is
$\operatorname{Cov}(B^{-1}\mathbf{X})=B^{-1}\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{X})B^{-\top}
=B^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}B^{-\top}=B^{-1}(BB^\top)B^{-\top}=I_p$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The running example, and the promised reversal.** Return to @exm-distance-two-trials, with
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}100&20\\20&16\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]$. Its inverse is
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}=\tfrac{1}{1200}\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}16&-20\\-20&100\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]$,
so the Mahalanobis quadratic form is $d_M^2=\tfrac{1}{75}\delta_1^2+\tfrac{1}{12}\delta_2^2
-\tfrac{1}{30}\delta_1\delta_2$. Evaluating on the two gaps $\boldsymbol{\delta}_P=(10,4)$ and
$\boldsymbol{\delta}_Q=(6,-4)$,
$$
d_M(P)=\sqrt{\tfrac{100}{75}+\tfrac{16}{12}-\tfrac{40}{30}}=\sqrt{1.333}=1.155,
\qquad
d_M(Q)=\sqrt{\tfrac{36}{75}+\tfrac{16}{12}+\tfrac{24}{30}}=\sqrt{2.613}=1.617 .
$$
Now the Mahalanobis distance ranks $P$ **ahead** of $Q$, the exact reverse of the raw and standardized
verdict. The reason is visible in the cross term. Study $P$ moved age and biomarker up together, the
direction the index correlation $\operatorname{corr}=0.5$ expects, so its cross term is negative
($-\tfrac{40}{30}$) and cancels much of the distance: a concordant move is cheap. Study $Q$ moved them in
opposite directions, against the correlation, so its cross term is positive ($+\tfrac{24}{30}$) and
*adds* to the distance: a discordant move is expensive. The standardized distance, blind to the
correlation, saw only that $Q$'s total standardized magnitude ($\sqrt{1.36}$) is smaller than $P$'s
($\sqrt2$) and called $Q$ closer; the Mahalanobis distance sees that $Q$'s *direction* is the improbable
one and calls $P$ closer. Which verdict should drive the decision is exactly the question
@sec-distance-bias settles, and the answer is "it depends on the unknown contrast." $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Mahalanobis is Euclidean in the right coordinates.** Equation @eq-distance-whitening says the
Mahalanobis distance measures the gap in coordinates where the covariate cloud has been sphered to an
isotropic unit ball. A direction in which the covariates are highly variable, or two covariates that move
together, are "cheap" to differ in, because such differences are expected under
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$; a direction of low variance, or a discordant move against a strong correlation, is
"expensive." Part 1 shows that standardized Euclidean distance is the special case that keeps the variances
but discards the correlations, that is, it whitens with the diagonal of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$. The worked
example of @sec-distance-example exhibits a candidate that standardized Euclidean distance and Mahalanobis
distance rank oppositely for exactly this reason. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The Mahalanobis distance is a genuine metric.** By @eq-distance-whitening, $d_M(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})=
\|B^{-1}(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\|_2$ is the Euclidean metric composed with the invertible linear map
$B^{-1}$; the symmetry, triangle inequality, and positive-definiteness of $d_M$ are inherited from those of
$\|\cdot\|_2$ because $B^{-1}$ is injective. The same argument makes $d_{SE}$ a metric. This is recorded as
part of @prp-distance-metric-properties. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This material corresponds to O.3 in the proof catalogue.

## Further distances {#sec-distance-variants}

The `uitc` toolkit offers several alternatives to the $\ell_2$ family, each answering a slightly different
question about the covariate gap. A reader in a hurry can treat this section as reference material: the
standardized Euclidean and Mahalanobis distances of the previous two sections are the workhorses, and the
variants here earn their place only when a specific question makes one of them apt (the single
worst-matched covariate, or mixed continuous and binary covariate types). Skip to @sec-distance-scale on a
first reading and return when a variant is needed.

::: {#def-distance-variants}
## Manhattan, Minkowski, mean-SMD, and Gower distances
With standardized gap components $z_{j\ell}=(\bar{x}_{j\ell}-\bar{x}_{0\ell})/s_\ell$ as in
@def-euclidean-distance, define:

The **Manhattan** (or $\ell_1$) distance, the sum of absolute standardized gaps,
$$
d_1\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;s\big)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}\big|z_{j\ell}\big|.
$$ {#eq-distance-manhattan}

The **Minkowski** distance of order $q\ge 1$, which interpolates between them,
$$
d_q\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;s\big)
=\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}\big|z_{j\ell}\big|^{q}\right)^{1/q},
\qquad
d_\infty=\max_{1\le\ell\le p}\big|z_{j\ell}\big| ,
$$ {#eq-distance-minkowski}
with $q=1$ the Manhattan distance, $q=2$ the standardized Euclidean distance, and the limit
$q\to\infty$ the **Chebyshev** distance, the largest single standardized gap.

The **mean absolute standardized mean difference** (mean-SMD), the Manhattan distance averaged over
covariates,
$$
d_{\mathrm{SMD}}\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;s\big)
=\frac1p\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}\big|z_{j\ell}\big|
=\frac1p\,d_1\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;s\big).
$$ {#eq-distance-meansmd}

The **Gower** distance, for mixed continuous and binary covariates, with a positive range $r_\ell$ for
each continuous covariate and binary covariates coded in $[0,1]$,
$$
d_G\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j\big)=\frac1p\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}g_{j\ell},
\qquad
g_{j\ell}=\begin{cases}
\min\!\big\{\,|\bar{x}_{j\ell}-\bar{x}_{0\ell}|/r_\ell,\ 1\,\big\}, & \ell\text{ continuous},\\[2pt]
|\bar{x}_{j\ell}-\bar{x}_{0\ell}|, & \ell\text{ binary}.
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-distance-gower}
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What each variant emphasizes, and what is excluded.** Raising the order $q$ concentrates attention on
the single worst-matched covariate: $d_\infty$ ignores all but the maximal standardized gap, so a
candidate with one badly mismatched covariate is penalized regardless of how well the rest agree, whereas
$d_1$ trades off freely across covariates. The mean-SMD rescales $d_1$ to the per-covariate average,
which makes it directly comparable across analyses with different numbers of covariates and ties the
diagnostic to the standardized-mean-difference balance tables of the propensity-score literature, where a
common rule of thumb flags any $|z_{j\ell}|>0.1$ as imbalance. The Gower distance handles continuous and
binary covariates on one footing by range-scaling and truncating the continuous gaps. The `uitc` toolkit
deliberately omits cosine, Hamming, Jaccard, Sorensen-Dice, and Haversine distances for this task: those
measure angular similarity, binary-set overlap, or geographic separation, none of which is the right notion
for a gap between continuous covariate means. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**A tiny Gower calculation.** Suppose a candidate is summarized by one continuous covariate, mean age, and
one binary covariate, proportion male. Let the pooled ages run from $40$ to $80$, so the age range is
$r_{\text{age}}=40$, and let the index means be age $60$ and proportion male $0.5$. A candidate reporting
mean age $68$ and proportion male $0.7$ has
$$
g_{\text{age}}=\min\!\Big\{\tfrac{|68-60|}{40},\,1\Big\}=\min\{0.2,\,1\}=0.2,
\qquad
g_{\text{male}}=|0.7-0.5|=0.2,
$$
and Gower distance $d_G=\tfrac12(0.2+0.2)=0.2$. The range division puts the $8$-year age gap on the same
$[0,1]$ footing as the $0.2$ difference in a proportion, and the truncation at $1$ means that even a wildly
out-of-range age gap (say a candidate with mean age $120$, giving $|120-60|/40=1.5$, capped to $1$) counts
no more than a complete binary disagreement. This is why Gower is the natural choice when continuous and
binary covariates must be compared together. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

For these to support a coherent "closest" in @def-comparator-selection, they should at least be genuine
distances. We record which are, and where the metric axioms can fail.

::: {#prp-distance-metric-properties}
## Metric properties of the covariate-summary distances
Fix the reference scales $s_\ell>0$, the covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ0$, and the Gower ranges
$r_\ell>0$. Then:

1. The standardized Euclidean distance $d_{SE}$ and the Mahalanobis distance $d_M$ are metrics on
$\mathbb{R}^p$.

2. For every $q\in[1,\infty]$ the Minkowski distance $d_q$ is a metric on $\mathbb{R}^p$; the mean-SMD
$d_{\mathrm{SMD}}=d_1/p$ is a metric. For $0<q<1$ the function in @eq-distance-minkowski is **not** a
metric: it violates the triangle inequality.

3. The Gower distance $d_G$ is a metric on the product covariate space.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Part 1.* By @def-euclidean-distance and @thm-mahalanobis-whitening, $d_{SE}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})=
\|S^{-1}(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\|_2$ and $d_M(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})=\|B^{-1}(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\|_2$
with $S^{-1}$ and $B^{-1}$ invertible. For any invertible linear map $T$, the function
$N(\mathbf{v})=\|T\mathbf{v}\|_2$ is a norm: it is absolutely homogeneous and satisfies the triangle
inequality because $\|\cdot\|_2$ does and $T$ is linear, and $N(\mathbf{v})=0$ forces $T\mathbf{v}=0$,
hence $\mathbf{v}=0$ by injectivity of $T$. A norm of a difference is a metric, giving part 1.

*Part 2.* For $q\in[1,\infty]$ the map $\mathbf{v}\mapsto\|\mathbf{v}\|_q$ is the $\ell_q$ norm, and
$d_q(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})=\|S^{-1}(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\|_q$ is the corresponding metric; the only
nontrivial axiom is the triangle inequality, which is Minkowski's inequality
$\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{w}\|_q\le\|\mathbf{u}\|_q+\|\mathbf{w}\|_q$. We verify the three orders this book
uses directly. For $q=1$ it is the triangle inequality for $|\cdot|$ summed over coordinates; for
$q=\infty$ it is $\max_\ell|u_\ell+w_\ell|\le\max_\ell(|u_\ell|+|w_\ell|)\le\max_\ell|u_\ell|+
\max_\ell|w_\ell|$; for $q=2$ it follows from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, since
$\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{w}\|_2^2=\|\mathbf{u}\|_2^2+2\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{w}+\|\mathbf{w}\|_2^2
\le\|\mathbf{u}\|_2^2+2\|\mathbf{u}\|_2\|\mathbf{w}\|_2+\|\mathbf{w}\|_2^2
=(\|\mathbf{u}\|_2+\|\mathbf{w}\|_2)^2$. For general $q\in[1,\infty)$ the inequality is the named Minkowski
inequality, which we cite here; its derivation from Hölder's inequality is exactly the content of
@exr-distance-minkowski-metric, so the single case not verified in the display above is signposted to a
worked exercise rather than left as a gap. Since $d_{\mathrm{SMD}}=d_1/p$ is a positive scalar multiple of
a metric, it is a metric.

For $0<q<1$ the triangle inequality fails. In $\mathbb{R}^2$ take $\mathbf{a}=(0,0)$, $\mathbf{b}=(1,0)$,
$\mathbf{c}=(1,1)$ with unit reference scales. Then $d_q(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c})=(1+1)^{1/q}=2^{1/q}$ while
$d_q(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})+d_q(\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c})=1+1=2$; since $1/q>1$ we have $2^{1/q}>2$, so the
direct distance exceeds the detour and the triangle inequality is violated.

*Part 3.* For a continuous coordinate, $\rho_\ell(a,b)=|a-b|/r_\ell$ is a metric on $\mathbb{R}$, and we
claim its truncation $\min\{\rho_\ell,1\}$ is again a metric. Symmetry and positive-definiteness are
immediate; for the triangle inequality, given points $a,b,c$, if either of $\min\{\rho_\ell(a,b),1\}$ or
$\min\{\rho_\ell(b,c),1\}$ equals $1$ then the right-hand side is at least $1\ge\min\{\rho_\ell(a,c),1\}$,
and otherwise both are below $1$, so $\rho_\ell(a,b),\rho_\ell(b,c)<1$ and
$\min\{\rho_\ell(a,c),1\}\le\rho_\ell(a,c)\le\rho_\ell(a,b)+\rho_\ell(b,c)
=\min\{\rho_\ell(a,b),1\}+\min\{\rho_\ell(b,c),1\}$. Thus each $g_\ell$ is a per-coordinate metric (the
binary case $|a-b|$ on $[0,1]$ being a metric outright). A nonnegative weighted sum of metrics composed
with coordinate projections is a pseudometric on the product, and it separates points here because each
$g_\ell(a_\ell,b_\ell)=0$ forces $a_\ell=b_\ell$; therefore $d_G=\frac1p\sum_\ell g_\ell$ is a metric.
$\square$
:::

This material corresponds to O.4 in the proof catalogue.

## Scale dependence and scale invariance {#sec-distance-scale}

A change in the unit of a covariate, age in months rather than years, weight in pounds rather than
kilograms, is a coordinate map $\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}$ with $A=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\dots,a_p)$
and $a_\ell>0$. A distance fit to drive a decision should not let such a relabeling change the decision.
The standardized and Mahalanobis families pass this test; the raw Euclidean distance fails it, and fails
it badly enough to reverse the ranking of candidates.

Here is the concrete picture behind the formal statement. Record age in months instead of years and you
multiply every age by $12$; but the standard deviation of age is *also* multiplied by $12$, so the
standardized age gap, the gap divided by that standard deviation, is unchanged, because the factor of $12$
cancels in the ratio. Re-expressing the same data in different units therefore cannot move a standardized
distance. That is all "coherent rescaling" means in the theorem below: the covariate and every auxiliary
input tied to its units (its reference scale, its Gower range, its row and column of the covariance
matrix) are re-expressed together, exactly as they would be in any honest re-recording of the data. The
practical stake is a regulatory one. A reviewer who asks "would your comparator choice have changed if the
sponsor had reported age in months rather than years?" is asking precisely whether the chosen distance is
scale-invariant, and the next theorem lets you answer "no, it could not have" for the standardized and
Mahalanobis families, while @prp-distance-scale-dependence shows you would have to answer "yes, possibly"
for the raw Euclidean distance.

::: {#thm-distance-scale-invariance}
## Scale invariance of standardized and Mahalanobis distances
Let $A=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\dots,a_p)$ with every $a_\ell>0$, and apply the **coherent rescaling**
that maps every summary vector $\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}$ and rescales the auxiliary inputs in step:
the reference scales $s_\ell\mapsto a_\ell s_\ell$ (so $S\mapsto AS$), the Gower ranges $r_\ell\mapsto
a_\ell r_\ell$, and the Mahalanobis covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mapsto A\boldsymbol{\Sigma}A$. Then the
standardized Euclidean distance $d_{SE}$, the Manhattan, Minkowski, and Chebyshev distances $d_q$
($q\in[1,\infty]$), the mean-SMD $d_{\mathrm{SMD}}$, the Gower distance $d_G$, and the Mahalanobis distance
$d_M$ are all unchanged. Moreover the Mahalanobis distance is invariant under **any** invertible affine
reparameterization $\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{c}$ with $A\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$
invertible, not only diagonal $A$, provided $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mapsto A\boldsymbol{\Sigma}A^\top$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Under the coherent rescaling the standardized components are unchanged coordinatewise: the rescaled gap is
$A\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j-A\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0=A\boldsymbol{\delta}_j$ with $\ell$-th entry
$a_\ell\delta_{j\ell}$, and dividing by the rescaled reference scale $a_\ell s_\ell$ gives
$$
\frac{a_\ell\,\delta_{j\ell}}{a_\ell s_\ell}=\frac{\delta_{j\ell}}{s_\ell}=z_{j\ell}.
$$
Every distance built from the standardized vector $\mathbf{z}_j$ alone, namely $d_{SE}=\|\mathbf{z}_j\|_2$,
$d_q=\|\mathbf{z}_j\|_q$ for $q\in[1,\infty]$, and $d_{\mathrm{SMD}}=\|\mathbf{z}_j\|_1/p$, is therefore a
function of unchanged quantities and is unchanged. For the Gower distance the continuous terms are
$\min\{a_\ell|\delta_{j\ell}|/(a_\ell r_\ell),1\}=\min\{|\delta_{j\ell}|/r_\ell,1\}$, unchanged, and the
binary terms involve no continuous unit, so $d_G$ is unchanged.

For the Mahalanobis distance, take the general invertible affine map $\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}+
\mathbf{c}$; the constant $\mathbf{c}$ cancels in the gap, which becomes $A\boldsymbol{\delta}_j$, and the
covariance becomes $A\boldsymbol{\Sigma}A^\top$. Using $(A\boldsymbol{\Sigma}A^\top)^{-1}=
A^{-\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}A^{-1}$,
$$
\big(A\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big)^\top\big(A\boldsymbol{\Sigma}A^\top\big)^{-1}\big(A\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big)
=\boldsymbol{\delta}_j^\top A^\top A^{-\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}A^{-1}A\,\boldsymbol{\delta}_j
=\boldsymbol{\delta}_j^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j ,
$$
so $d_M$ is unchanged. The diagonal coherent rescaling is the special case $A=\operatorname{diag}(a_\ell)$,
for which $A\boldsymbol{\Sigma}A=A\boldsymbol{\Sigma}A^\top$. $\square$
:::

The raw Euclidean distance enjoys none of this. It is not merely rescaled by a unit change; the rescaling
reweights the covariates unequally and can overturn which candidate is judged closest.

::: {#prp-distance-scale-dependence}
## Raw Euclidean distance is scale-dependent and can reverse rankings
Let $A=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\dots,a_p)$ with $a_\ell>0$. In general
$d_E(A\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,A\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j)\ne d_E(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j)$, because
$$
d_E\big(A\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,A\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j\big)^2=\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}a_\ell^2\,\delta_{j\ell}^2 ,
$$ {#eq-distance-rescaled}
a reweighting of the squared gaps by $a_\ell^2$. There exist two candidates whose raw-Euclidean ranking is
reversed by a change of units in a single covariate.
:::

::: {.proof}
Equation @eq-distance-rescaled is immediate from $A\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j-A\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0=
A\boldsymbol{\delta}_j$ and the diagonal form of $A$. For the reversal, take $p=2$ and two candidates with
gaps $\boldsymbol{\delta}_1=(1,2)$ and $\boldsymbol{\delta}_2=(2,1)$. With unit scaling both have squared
distance $1^2+2^2=2^2+1^2=5$, so they tie. Rescale the first coordinate by $a_1=10$ and keep $a_2=1$.
Then
$$
d_E(A\boldsymbol{\delta}_1)^2=10^2\cdot1+1\cdot4=104,
\qquad
d_E(A\boldsymbol{\delta}_2)^2=10^2\cdot4+1\cdot1=401 ,
$$
so candidate $1$ is now strictly closer than candidate $2$, whereas before they were equidistant; a unit
change has manufactured a strict preference. Perturbing $\boldsymbol{\delta}_1$ to $(1,2+\varepsilon)$ for
small $\varepsilon>0$ makes candidate $2$ strictly closer under unit scaling ($5<5+4\varepsilon+
\varepsilon^2$) while candidate $1$ remains strictly closer after the rescaling, an outright reversal of
the strict ranking. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The decision-theoretic moral.** Because the comparator-selection rule @eq-distance-argmin returns an
$\arg\min$, only the *ranking* of candidates matters, and @prp-distance-scale-dependence shows the raw
Euclidean ranking is an artifact of the recording units. Standardized Euclidean and Mahalanobis distances
are immune (@thm-distance-scale-invariance), which is why `uitc` recommends them whenever covariates carry
mixed units. The worked example of @sec-distance-example exhibits a concrete reversal: raw Euclidean
distance there selects the candidate with the *largest* eventual bias, precisely because it is dominated by
a large-unit covariate. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This material corresponds to O.5 in the proof catalogue.

## Bias bounds from covariate-summary distance {#sec-distance-bias}

A distance is worth minimizing only if minimizing it reduces the bias of the eventual estimate. We now
prove exactly when it does. Throughout this section we work under conditional constancy, so that the
conditional contrast (or, in the unanchored case, each conditional mean) is the same function of the
covariates in the index and comparator populations; the only cross-population difference is the covariate
distribution. The quantity of interest is the **transport bias**
$$
B_j\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_j}\big[\tau(\mathbf{X})\big]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_0}\big[\tau(\mathbf{X})\big],
$$ {#eq-distance-bias-def}
the difference between the marginal effect over the comparator population $\mathcal{P}_j$ and the marginal
effect over the index population $\mathcal{P}_0$, where $\tau$ is the shared conditional contrast. Under
conditional constancy this $B_j$ is the residual bias incurred by treating comparator $j$'s population as a
stand-in for the index population, or equivalently the bias that remains if the covariate gap
$\boldsymbol{\delta}_j$ is left unadjusted; it is the quantity that population adjustment
(@thm-unanchored-paic-consistency) is designed to remove.

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation of the two working assumptions.** Two phrases carry this whole section. *Conditional
constancy* (@def-conditional-constancy-relative; in the unanchored case the stronger
@def-conditional-constancy-absolute) means the conditional contrast $\tau(\mathbf{x})$, the
treatment effect among patients whose covariates equal $\mathbf{x}$, is the **same function** of
$\mathbf{x}$ in the index and comparator populations; what differs between the populations is only how many
patients sit at each value of $\mathbf{x}$. If that holds, the sole thing a comparator's population changes
is the covariate mix, so any transport bias is due entirely to the covariate gap. *Transport bias* $B_j$
is then just the difference between the average effect you would report over the comparator's patient mix
and the average effect over the index patient mix: it is what you get wrong by handing an estimand defined
for the index population to a population with a different covariate distribution. A small covariate
distance is our attempt to keep that difference small; the rest of the section is about when it succeeds.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

### The linear case: an exact Cauchy-Schwarz bound {#sec-distance-bias-linear}

When the contrast is affine, the bias is a linear functional of the covariate-mean gap, and the
quadratic-form distances bound it sharply.

What does "affine contrast" mean for a real outcome, and when is it plausible? Fit an outcome model on the
link scale, the logit (log-odds) scale for a binary response, the log scale for a hazard, with a linear
predictor of the Chapter 20 form $\eta=\mu+\boldsymbol{\beta}_1^\top\mathbf{x}+(\gamma+\boldsymbol{\beta}_2
^\top\mathbf{x})\,T$, where $T$ is the treatment indicator. The conditional contrast on that scale, the
treatment effect at covariate value $\mathbf{x}$, is
$$
\tau(\mathbf{x})=\eta\big|_{T=1}-\eta\big|_{T=0}=\gamma+\boldsymbol{\beta}_2^\top\mathbf{x},
$$
which is affine in $\mathbf{x}$ with intercept $\alpha=\gamma$ and slope vector
$\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{\beta}_2$. So in the theorem below $\alpha$ is the treatment effect at
$\mathbf{x}=\mathbf 0$ and $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is the vector of **effect-modifier slopes**: each
$\beta_\ell$ says how much the treatment's effect on the link scale changes per unit of covariate $\ell$.
The affine case is therefore exactly "a linear outcome model on the link scale whose treatment effect is
modified linearly by the covariates, with no covariate-by-covariate or higher-order terms." It is a
reasonable working hypothesis when effect modification is mild and roughly linear, and it is the sensitivity
input under which comparator distance provably bounds bias. Two poles are worth noting: if
$\boldsymbol{\beta}=\mathbf 0$ there is no effect modification and the transport bias is zero for *any*
covariate gap; the entire difficulty lives in the direction of $\boldsymbol{\beta}\ne\mathbf 0$, which is
why the theorem's bound pairs the gap with $\boldsymbol{\beta}$.

::: {#thm-distance-linear-bias-bound}
## Linear bias bound
Suppose the shared conditional contrast is affine in the covariates,
$\tau(\mathbf{x})=\alpha+\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\mathbf{x}$. Then the transport bias @eq-distance-bias-def
is the linear functional of the covariate-mean gap
$$
B_j=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\delta}_j
=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0\big),
$$ {#eq-distance-bias-linear}
and it is bounded by either quadratic-form distance:

1. with $S=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\dots,s_p)$,
$$
|B_j|\;\le\;\|S\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2\;\cdot\;d_{SE}\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;s\big),
$$ {#eq-distance-bias-se}
with equality if and only if the standardized gap $\mathbf{z}_j=S^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j$ is parallel
to $S\boldsymbol{\beta}$;

2. with $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ0$,
$$
|B_j|\;\le\;\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta}}\;\cdot\;
d_M\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\big)
=\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\cdot\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}},
$$ {#eq-distance-bias-mah}
with equality if and only if $\boldsymbol{\delta}_j$ is parallel to $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The intercept $\alpha$ cancels in the difference @eq-distance-bias-def, leaving
$B_j=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_j}[\mathbf{X}]-\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_0}[\mathbf{X}]=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0)
=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\delta}_j$, which is @eq-distance-bias-linear.

*Bound 1.* Insert $S^{-1}S=I$: $B_j=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top S S^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j=
(S\boldsymbol{\beta})^\top\mathbf{z}_j$. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality in $\mathbb{R}^p$,
$$
|B_j|=\big|(S\boldsymbol{\beta})^\top\mathbf{z}_j\big|
\le\|S\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2\,\|\mathbf{z}_j\|_2
=\|S\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2\,d_{SE}\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;s\big),
$$
which is @eq-distance-bias-se. Cauchy-Schwarz holds with equality if and only if the two vectors are
linearly dependent, that is, $\mathbf{z}_j\parallel S\boldsymbol{\beta}$.

*Bound 2.* Write $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}$ with the
symmetric square root of @thm-cov-psd and insert $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}=I$:
$$
B_j=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\delta}_j
=\big(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\beta}\big)^\top
\big(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big).
$$
By Cauchy-Schwarz,
$$
|B_j|\le\big\|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\beta}\big\|_2
\big\|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\big\|_2
=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta}}\,
\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\delta}_j^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j}
=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta}}\;
d_M\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j;\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\big),
$$
which is @eq-distance-bias-mah, using @eq-distance-mahalanobis for the last factor. Equality holds if and
only if $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\parallel\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}
\boldsymbol{\beta}$; applying the invertible map $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}$ to both sides, this is
$\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\parallel\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta}$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reading the bounds.** Both bounds factor the bias into a fixed coefficient magnitude, $\|S
\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2$ or $\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$, which does not depend on the
candidate, times a distance, which does. Because the coefficient factor is common to all candidates, each
distance ranks the candidates exactly by its own bound on $|B_j|$: selecting the
$d_{SE}$-minimizer minimizes the standardized bound, and selecting the $d_M$-minimizer minimizes the
Mahalanobis bound. The two bounds need not agree on the winner, because $\|S\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2\,d_{SE}$
and $\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\,d_M$ are different upper bounds on the same $|B_j|$; the
equality conditions say each bound is tight for the candidate whose gap aligns with the coefficient vector
in the relevant geometry. This is not a defect but the precise sense in which the right distance is the one
matched to the unknown contrast direction $\boldsymbol{\beta}$, a point the worked example makes concrete
and the caveat of @sec-distance-caveat makes unavoidable. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Connection to unanchored consistency.** The transport bias @eq-distance-bias-def is the population-level
obstacle in the unanchored PAIC theorem @thm-unanchored-paic-consistency. That theorem recovers the target
estimand only when every imbalanced effect modifier and prognostic variable is balanced, so that no
residual covariate gap survives; its necessity clause exhibits the bias as an integral that is nonzero
exactly when an imbalanced covariate is omitted. Under the affine specialization
$\tau(\mathbf{x})=\alpha+\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\mathbf{x}$ (for instance affine conditional means on the
identity scale, as in hypothesis (v) "sufficiency of the matched moments" of
@thm-anchored-maic-consistency), that integral collapses to an inner product of the form
@eq-distance-bias-linear, and @thm-distance-linear-bias-bound bounds it by the covariate-summary distance.
Comparator selection therefore *bounds the very bias the consistency theorem assumes away*: a smaller
distance means a smaller worst-case residual bias, under linearity. The qualifier "under linearity" is
essential, and @sec-distance-bias-nonlinear and @sec-distance-caveat show what happens without it. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The running example: exact bias and the two bounds.** Suppose, as a sensitivity input, the effect-modifier
slopes are $\boldsymbol{\beta}=(0.1,\,0.5)$, that is, the treatment's effect on the link scale rises by
$0.1$ per year of age and by $0.5$ per biomarker unit. Then the exact transport biases of
@exm-distance-two-trials are
$$
B_P=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\delta}_P=0.1(10)+0.5(4)=3.0,
\qquad
B_Q=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\delta}_Q=0.1(6)+0.5(-4)=-1.4 .
$$
The standardized Cauchy-Schwarz bound uses $S\boldsymbol{\beta}=(1,2)$, so
$\|S\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2=\sqrt5=2.236$, giving $|B_P|\le 2.236(1.414)=3.16$ and $|B_Q|\le2.236(1.166)=2.61$;
the Mahalanobis bound uses $\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\sqrt7=2.646$, giving $|B_P|\le2.646(1.155)=3.06$ and
$|B_Q|\le2.646(1.617)=4.28$. Both bounds dominate the exact biases, as they must. Now the honest lesson:
the **standardized** winner $Q$ has the *smaller* true bias ($1.4$ against $3.0$), while the
**Mahalanobis** winner $P$ has the *larger* true bias, so for this particular $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ the
standardized distance was the faithful ranker and Mahalanobis was misled. With slopes of opposite sign,
for example $\boldsymbol{\beta}=(-0.1,\,0.5)$, the verdict flips: $B_P=1.0$ and $B_Q=-2.6$, and Mahalanobis
is the faithful ranker. Since $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is unknown when the comparator is chosen, no
distance is guaranteed to rank by bias; this is exactly @prp-distance-diagnostic-not-validity, previewed
here in arithmetic. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Bias against variance: the effective-sample-size tradeoff.** The gap $\boldsymbol{\delta}_j$ costs in two
ways. Any part of it left unadjusted contributes bias, capped under linearity by the bounds above; the part
that is matched costs precision, because the subsequent unanchored MAIC reweights the index sample (size
$n$) to the comparator's means, and a larger standardized gap typically forces more extreme weights and
hence a smaller effective sample size $\mathrm{ESS}=(\sum_i w_i)^2/\sum_i w_i^2$ (@thm-maic-ess-bound), inflating the variance by the
factor $n/\mathrm{ESS}$. The schematic pattern, for an index study of $n=200$, is

| candidate | $d_{SE}$ | typical weight extremity | illustrative $\mathrm{ESS}$ | variance inflation $n/\mathrm{ESS}$ |
|:--|--:|:--|--:|--:|
| close (Study $Q$) | $1.17$ | mild | $150$ | $1.33$ |
| moderate (Study $P$) | $1.41$ | moderate | $110$ | $1.82$ |
| far (hypothetical) | $3.0$ | severe | $35$ | $5.7$ |

: How the mean distance drives the effective sample size after reweighting. The $\mathrm{ESS}$ column is illustrative: the true value depends on the index individual patient data, not on the means alone. {#tbl-distance-ess}

Two consequences. First, in the linear case there is usually no dramatic conflict: the minimum-distance
candidate tends to minimize both the residual-bias bound and the reweighting variance at once. The genuine
tension appears among candidates of *comparable* distance, where one breaks the tie by projected
$\mathrm{ESS}$, and in how many covariates to match: because a far comparator's variance can explode (bottom
row), a mean-squared-error view, $\mathrm{MSE}\approx \text{bias}^2+\text{variance}$, can prefer leaving a
weakly modifying covariate unmatched, accepting its bounded bias, over the variance cost of matching it. Second, and
more important, the distance bounds bias only under linearity; a close, high-$\mathrm{ESS}$ comparator can
still be badly biased through nonlinearity or unmeasured imbalance (@sec-distance-caveat). The defensible
practice is to report distance and projected $\mathrm{ESS}$ together and to choose on the mean-squared-error
picture, not on distance alone. This trade-off is developed as @exr-distance-ess-tradeoff and connects to
the simulation estimands of Chapter 29. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

### The nonlinear case: a Lipschitz-Wasserstein bound {#sec-distance-bias-nonlinear}

The punchline of this subsection first, because it is easy to lose in the machinery: the clean linear bound
of @thm-distance-linear-bias-bound has **no analogue at the level of covariate means** once the contrast is
nonlinear. A bias bound still exists, but it needs a distance between whole distributions, not between their
centers, and no distance between means can supply it. This is the deepest reason aggregate distance matching
is a diagnostic and not a transportability theorem, and the rest of the section makes it precise.

When the contrast is not affine, the mean gap no longer determines the bias, because a nonlinear $\tau$
responds to the whole distribution and not only its center. A bias bound survives, but the distance it
requires is between full distributions.

Before the formal statement, here is the object in plain terms. A **coupling** of the index and comparator
covariate distributions is a way of pairing each comparator patient with an index patient, that is, a joint
distribution whose two margins are the two populations. Picture the comparator patients as piles of sand
sitting at their covariate values and the index patients as holes to be filled at theirs; a coupling is a
transport plan saying how much sand moves from each pile to each hole. The **Wasserstein-1 distance**
$W_\rho(\mathcal{P}_j,\mathcal{P}_0)$ is the cost of the cheapest such plan, where moving one unit of mass a
covariate-distance $\rho$ costs $\rho$: it is the minimum average distance patients must be shifted in
covariate space to turn one population's covariate distribution into the other's. Unlike a gap between
means, it sees the whole shape of each distribution, its spread and its tails, not only its center. For
instance, to turn a population with everyone at $x=0$ into one split evenly between $x=-1$ and $x=+1$, half
the mass moves one unit left and half moves one unit right, an average move of $1$, so $W_\rho=1$, even
though the two means agree at $0$; this is the example of @prp-distance-diagnostic-not-validity. The next
theorem says a **Lipschitz** contrast, one that cannot change faster than a fixed rate $L$ as the covariates
change, can differ across two populations by at most $L$ times this transport cost.

::: {#thm-lipschitz-bias-bound}
## Lipschitz bias bound via the Wasserstein distance
Let $(\mathcal{X},\rho)$ be a metric space and let $\mathcal{P}_0,\mathcal{P}_j$ be probability measures on
$\mathcal{X}$ with finite first moment. Suppose the conditional contrast $\tau:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}$ is
$L$-Lipschitz with respect to $\rho$, that is $|\tau(\mathbf{x})-\tau(\mathbf{x}')|\le L\,\rho(\mathbf{x},
\mathbf{x}')$ for all $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}'$. Then the transport bias is bounded by the Wasserstein-1
distance,
$$
\big|B_j\big|
=\Big|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_j}[\tau]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_0}[\tau]\Big|
\;\le\;L\;W_\rho\big(\mathcal{P}_j,\mathcal{P}_0\big),
\qquad
W_\rho(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{Q})=\inf_{\gamma\in\Pi(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{Q})}\int\rho(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})
\,d\gamma(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}),
$$ {#eq-distance-lipschitz}
where $\Pi(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{Q})$ is the set of couplings of $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{Q}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $\gamma\in\Pi(\mathcal{P}_j,\mathcal{P}_0)$ be any coupling, that is, a joint law of a pair
$(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ whose first marginal is $\mathcal{P}_j$ and whose second marginal is
$\mathcal{P}_0$. Because the marginals reproduce the two expectations,
$$
B_j=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_j}[\tau]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_0}[\tau]
=\mathbb{E}_\gamma\big[\tau(\mathbf{X})-\tau(\mathbf{Y})\big].
$$
Taking absolute values, then using Jensen's inequality for the convex function $|\cdot|$
(@thm-jensen) and the Lipschitz hypothesis,
$$
|B_j|=\big|\mathbb{E}_\gamma[\tau(\mathbf{X})-\tau(\mathbf{Y})]\big|
\le\mathbb{E}_\gamma\big|\tau(\mathbf{X})-\tau(\mathbf{Y})\big|
\le L\,\mathbb{E}_\gamma\big[\rho(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})\big].
$$
This holds for every coupling $\gamma$, so taking the infimum over $\gamma\in\Pi(\mathcal{P}_j,
\mathcal{P}_0)$ of the right-hand side gives $|B_j|\le L\,W_\rho(\mathcal{P}_j,\mathcal{P}_0)$, which is
@eq-distance-lipschitz. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why the Wasserstein distance is the right yardstick (Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality).** The bound
@eq-distance-lipschitz used a single coupling; remarkably, the best possible bound of this shape is again a
Wasserstein distance. The Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality states
$$
W_\rho(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{Q})=\sup_{\|f\|_{\mathrm{Lip}_\rho}\le1}
\big|\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{P}f-\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{Q}f\big|,
$$
where the supremum runs over all functions $f$ that are $1$-Lipschitz with respect to $\rho$, meaning $f$
changes by at most the distance between its inputs ($\|f\|_{\mathrm{Lip}_\rho}$ is the smallest such rate).
Read from right to left, it says the Wasserstein distance *is* the worst-case transport bias over every
$1$-Lipschitz contrast: no unit-Lipschitz contrast can separate the two populations by more than $W_\rho$,
and some contrast comes arbitrarily close. That is exactly why $W_\rho$, and not some cruder distributional
distance, is the natural yardstick for Lipschitz transport bias, and why the bound in terms of it cannot be
improved. Applying the identity to $f=\tau/L$ recovers @eq-distance-lipschitz. We gave the elementary
coupling proof above because it is self-contained and needs only @thm-jensen; the duality is recorded here
for the reader who wants to know the bound is tight, not merely valid. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The decisive point is that a distance between means is **not** a Wasserstein distance between
distributions. It is only a lower bound on it, so a small mean distance does not imply a small Wasserstein
distance, hence does not bound the nonlinear bias.

::: {#prp-distance-wasserstein-lower-bound}
## Mean distance lower-bounds the Wasserstein distance
With $\rho$ the Euclidean metric on $\mathbb{R}^p$, the Euclidean distance between covariate means is
dominated by the Wasserstein-1 distance between the covariate distributions:
$$
d_E\big(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j\big)
=\big\|\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0\big\|_2
\;\le\;W_\rho\big(\mathcal{P}_j,\mathcal{P}_0\big).
$$ {#eq-distance-wlower}
Consequently a small Wasserstein distance forces a small mean distance, but a small (or zero) mean distance
places no upper bound on the Wasserstein distance, and hence none on the nonlinear bias of
@eq-distance-lipschitz.
:::

::: {.proof}
For any coupling $\gamma$ of $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ with marginals $\mathcal{P}_j,\mathcal{P}_0$, the
vector Jensen inequality (@thm-jensen applied to the convex norm $\|\cdot\|_2$) gives
$$
\big\|\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0\big\|_2
=\big\|\mathbb{E}_\gamma[\mathbf{X}-\mathbf{Y}]\big\|_2
\le\mathbb{E}_\gamma\big\|\mathbf{X}-\mathbf{Y}\big\|_2
=\mathbb{E}_\gamma\big[\rho(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})\big].
$$
Taking the infimum over couplings gives @eq-distance-wlower. The implication is one-directional: the
example in @prp-distance-diagnostic-not-validity has $d_E=0$ yet $W_\rho>0$ and nonzero bias, so no reverse
inequality can hold. $\square$
:::

This material corresponds to O.6 in the proof catalogue.

## Distance is a diagnostic, not a validity guarantee {#sec-distance-caveat}

We now state and prove the chapter's central caveat. Every distance of this chapter is a function of the
reported covariate summaries; the means are the universally available summary, and all of the distances
reduce to zero when the means coincide. The next proposition shows that zero distance carries no guarantee
about the target effect, in two independent ways: through nonlinearity, which the means cannot see, and
through unmeasured variables, which no observed summary can see.

::: {#prp-distance-diagnostic-not-validity}
## Zero covariate-summary distance does not bound transport bias
Let $d$ be any covariate-summary distance of this chapter that is computed from the covariate means alone:
Euclidean, standardized Euclidean, Mahalanobis, Manhattan, Minkowski, mean-SMD, or Gower with the means as
inputs.

1. **(Nonlinearity.)** There exist populations $\mathcal{P}_0,\mathcal{P}_j$ with identical covariate
means, hence $d(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j)=0$ for every such $d$, and a conditional contrast
$\tau$ for which the target effects differ, $\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_j}[\tau]\ne\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_0}
[\tau]$. Consequently no inequality of the form $|B_j|\le C\,d(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j)$ can
hold for a finite constant $C$ uniformly over contrasts; the transport bias is not a function of any
mean-based distance.

2. **(Unmeasured imbalance.)** There exist populations whose observed covariate $\mathbf{X}$ has identical
distributions, hence zero distance under every summary of $\mathbf{X}$, that nonetheless differ in an
unobserved prognostic variable $W$ in a way that makes the unanchored target means
$\mathbb{E}[\mu_t(\mathbf{X},W)]$ differ across populations.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Part 1.* Let the covariate be scalar. Let $\mathcal{P}_0$ place all mass at $X=0$, and let
$\mathcal{P}_j$ place mass $\tfrac12$ at $X=-1$ and mass $\tfrac12$ at $X=+1$. Both have mean
$\bar{x}_0=\bar{x}_j=0$, so every mean-based distance is zero. Take the nonlinear contrast
$\tau(x)=x^2$. Then
$$
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_0}[\tau]=0^2=0,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_j}[\tau]=\tfrac12(-1)^2+\tfrac12(1)^2=1,
$$
so $B_j=1\ne0$ while $d=0$. Since $|B_j|=1>C\cdot0$ for every finite $C$, no bound of the stated form can
hold. It is worth seeing this against @thm-lipschitz-bias-bound in full. On the support $\{-1,0,1\}$ the
contrast $\tau(x)=x^2$ is Lipschitz: for any two points $|x^2-y^2|=|x+y|\,|x-y|\le 2|x-y|$, so we may take
$L=2$. The Wasserstein distance is $W_\rho(\mathcal{P}_j,\mathcal{P}_0)=1$, by the following explicit
transport plan: move the mass $\tfrac12$ sitting at $x=-1$ to $x=0$ (a shift of distance $1$) and the mass
$\tfrac12$ sitting at $x=+1$ to $x=0$ (a shift of distance $1$), for an average move of
$\tfrac12\cdot1+\tfrac12\cdot1=1$; no plan does better, since all the mass of $\mathcal{P}_j$ must arrive at
the single point $0$ where $\mathcal{P}_0$ lives, each unit travelling at least distance $1$. The Lipschitz
bound then reads
$$
|B_j|=1\;\le\;L\,W_\rho=2\cdot1=2 ,
$$
which holds with room to spare, while the mean distance $d_E=0$ vanishes. The bias is real, it is controlled
by the full-distribution distance, and it is wholly invisible to the means: it hides in the spread, which no
mean-based distance records.

*Part 2.* Let the observed covariate $\mathbf{X}$ have the same law in $\mathcal{P}_0$ and $\mathcal{P}_j$,
and let an unobserved prognostic variable $W$, which one should picture concretely as ECOG performance
status, a strong prognostic factor in oncology that the single-arm Phase II might record but that the
external Phase III reports only partially or on an incompatible scale, so it never enters the shared
covariate table, have mean $\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_0}[W]=0$ in the index population and
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_j}[W]=1$ in the comparator population, with $W$ independent of $\mathbf{X}$ in each. Let the conditional mean depend on $W$, for instance $\mu_t(\mathbf{x},w)=w$ for the
relevant arm. Every distance computed from $\mathbf{X}$ is zero because the laws of $\mathbf{X}$ agree, yet
the unanchored target means differ:
$$
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_0}[\mu_t(\mathbf{X},W)]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_0}[W]=0,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_j}[\mu_t(\mathbf{X},W)]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_j}[W]=1.
$$
This is exactly the omitted-prognostic-variable bias of @thm-unanchored-paic-consistency: with $W$ absent
from the adjustment set, the inner difference of its necessity integral @eq-pat-unanchored-bias does not
vanish, and no comparator term cancels it in the unanchored contrast. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What aggregate-level matching is, and is not, good for.** Parts 1 and 2 of
@prp-distance-diagnostic-not-validity delimit the method precisely. Aggregate-level distance matching
*is* a sound basis for: a **comparator-selection rule** when several bridging studies are available
(@def-comparator-selection); an **overlap diagnostic** to be inspected before any unanchored MAIC, STC, or
ML-UMR, since a large distance forewarns of heavy reweighting and low effective sample size
(@thm-maic-ess-bound); and a **sensitivity-analysis input** that names which covariates drive the bridge.
It is *not* a substitute for adjusting every imbalanced effect modifier (@def-effect-modifier) and
prognostic variable (@def-prognostic-variable); it is not a proof of the shared prognostic factor
assumption (@def-spfa); it is not a proof of conditional constancy of absolute effects
(@def-conditional-constancy-absolute); and it is no guard whatever against unmeasured imbalance. It
presupposes, and does not establish, the clinical and design comparability of the trials, which must be
judged separately and before any distance is computed (step 3 of @sec-distance-workflow): two studies can
match on age, sex, and biomarker means and still differ in line of therapy, outcome definition, follow-up,
or standard of care, and no small distance repairs that. The quantitative bias analysis of Chapter 28 is
the tool for the residual and unmeasured part that distance matching leaves untouched. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Second-moment distances narrow, but do not close, the gap.** Part 1 exploits that the means agree while
the variances differ. One can blunt this particular counterexample by augmenting the summary with second
moments and using a distance that also compares the covariances, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0$ against
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$; this is the diagnostic analogue of MAIC second-moment balancing
(Chapter 18) and of the joint-distribution modeling that ML-NMR achieves through a copula
(@def-gaussian-copula, Chapter 22). But no finite collection of moments closes the gap for every
contrast: @exr-distance-secondmoment constructs two populations matching in mean *and* variance whose
target effects differ under a quartic contrast, and Part 2 shows that unmeasured variables defeat any
summary of the observed covariates regardless of how many moments it includes. Distance matching on
richer summaries is a better diagnostic, never a validity proof. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This material corresponds to O.7 in the proof catalogue.

## A fully worked example: ranking four comparators {#sec-distance-example}

We rank four candidate comparator studies for a single-arm index study, computing every distance and the
exact bias by hand, and exhibit the chapter's three lessons at once: the raw Euclidean ranking is an
artifact of units, the standardized and Mahalanobis distances disagree because of covariate correlation,
and the distance that tracks the actual bias is the one matched to the contrast direction.

::: {#exm-distance-comparator-ranking}
## Selecting among four comparator studies
The index single-arm study reports covariate means on three baseline covariates, mean age
(years), proportion male, and mean biomarker level (units),
$$
\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0=(60,\;0.5,\;10),
$$
with reference scales $s=(10,\;0.5,\;4)$ (the biomarker and age standard deviations from the index IPD, and
the Bernoulli standard deviation $\sqrt{0.5\cdot0.5}=0.5$ for sex), and index covariance
$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{pmatrix}100&0&20\\[1pt]0&0.25&0\\[1pt]20&0&16\end{pmatrix},
$$
in which age and biomarker are positively correlated, $\operatorname{corr}=20/(10\cdot4)=0.5$, and sex is
uncorrelated with both. (This $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ0$: its leading minors are $100>0$,
$100\cdot0.25=25>0$, and $\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=0.25\,(100\cdot16-20^2)=300>0$.) Four candidate
comparator studies report means $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_A,\dots,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_D$, with covariate gaps
$\boldsymbol{\delta}_j=\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0$ and standardized gaps
$\mathbf{z}_j=S^{-1}\boldsymbol{\delta}_j$:
$$
\begin{array}{llll}
\text{Study } A: & \boldsymbol{\delta}_A=(12,\;0.05,\;1), & \mathbf{z}_A=(1.2,\;0.1,\;0.25),\\
\text{Study } B: & \boldsymbol{\delta}_B=(6,\;0.30,\;4.8), & \mathbf{z}_B=(0.6,\;0.6,\;1.2),\\
\text{Study } C: & \boldsymbol{\delta}_C=(1,\;0.45,\;6), & \mathbf{z}_C=(0.1,\;0.9,\;1.5),\\
\text{Study } D: & \boldsymbol{\delta}_D=(8,\;0.20,\;4), & \mathbf{z}_D=(0.8,\;0.4,\;1.0).
\end{array}
$$

**Raw Euclidean (@eq-distance-euclidean).** Squaring and summing the raw gaps,
$$
d_E(A)=\sqrt{12^2+0.05^2+1^2}=\sqrt{145.00}=12.04,
\quad
d_E(B)=\sqrt{6^2+0.3^2+4.8^2}=\sqrt{59.13}=7.69,
$$
$$
