d_E(C)=\sqrt{1^2+0.45^2+6^2}=\sqrt{37.20}=6.10,
\quad
d_E(D)=\sqrt{8^2+0.2^2+4^2}=\sqrt{80.04}=8.95.
$$
The raw ranking is $C\prec B\prec D\prec A$, so raw Euclidean distance selects **Study $C$**.

**Standardized Euclidean (@eq-distance-stdeuclidean).** Using the standardized gaps,
$$
d_{SE}(A)=\sqrt{1.2^2+0.1^2+0.25^2}=\sqrt{1.5125}=1.230,
\quad
d_{SE}(B)=\sqrt{0.6^2+0.6^2+1.2^2}=\sqrt{2.16}=1.470,
$$
$$
d_{SE}(C)=\sqrt{0.1^2+0.9^2+1.5^2}=\sqrt{3.07}=1.752,
\quad
d_{SE}(D)=\sqrt{0.8^2+0.4^2+1.0^2}=\sqrt{1.80}=1.342.
$$
The standardized ranking is $A\prec D\prec B\prec C$, so standardized Euclidean distance selects
**Study $A$**: the opposite winner from the raw distance. The reversal is intuitive. Study $A$'s
$12$-year age gap dominates the raw distance, but in standard-deviation units it is only $1.2$ SD; Study
$C$'s age gap is only $1$ year, so it looks closest on the raw scale, which age dominates, yet its sex and
biomarker gaps are large when standardized ($0.9$ and $1.5$ SD), and the raw distance, blind to scale,
mistakes $C$ for the closest.

**Mahalanobis (@eq-distance-mahalanobis).** With
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$ having entries $(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1})_{11}=\tfrac{1}{75}$,
$(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1})_{22}=4$, $(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1})_{33}=\tfrac{1}{12}$, and
$(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1})_{13}=-\tfrac{1}{60}$ (from inverting the age-biomarker block
$\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}100&20\\20&16\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]$, of determinant $1200$, and the scalar
sex block), the quadratic form is $d_M^2=\tfrac{1}{75}\delta_1^2+4\delta_2^2+\tfrac{1}{12}\delta_3^2
-\tfrac{1}{30}\delta_1\delta_3$. Evaluating,
$$
d_M(A)=\sqrt{1.613}=1.270,
\quad
d_M(B)=\sqrt{1.800}=1.342,
\quad
d_M(C)=\sqrt{3.623}=1.904,
\quad
d_M(D)=\sqrt{1.280}=1.131.
$$
The Mahalanobis ranking is $D\prec A\prec B\prec C$, so Mahalanobis distance selects **Study $D$**: a
third, distinct winner. The reason is the age-biomarker correlation. Study $D$'s gap $(8,0.2,4)$ moves age
and biomarker up together, exactly the direction the index covariance expects, so it is "cheap" in
Mahalanobis geometry; standardized Euclidean distance, ignoring the correlation, charges $D$ for both
moves separately and ranks it behind $A$.

**Mean-SMD (@eq-distance-meansmd).** Averaging the absolute standardized gaps,
$d_{\mathrm{SMD}}(A)=1.55/3=0.517$, $d_{\mathrm{SMD}}(B)=2.40/3=0.800$, $d_{\mathrm{SMD}}(C)=2.50/3=0.833$,
$d_{\mathrm{SMD}}(D)=2.20/3=0.733$, giving the ranking $A\prec D\prec B\prec C$, the same as standardized
Euclidean; the $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ rankings often agree, though they need not.

The four criteria are collected below; each column's minimum is the selected study.

| Study | raw $d_E$ | std $d_{SE}$ | mean-SMD | Mahalanobis $d_M$ |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| $A$ | $12.04$ | $\mathbf{1.230}$ | $\mathbf{0.517}$ | $1.270$ |
| $B$ | $7.69$  | $1.470$ | $0.800$ | $1.342$ |
| $C$ | $\mathbf{6.10}$  | $1.752$ | $0.833$ | $1.904$ |
| $D$ | $8.95$  | $1.342$ | $0.733$ | $\mathbf{1.131}$ |

**Which winner is right? The bias bound decides.** Suppose, as a sensitivity input, the unanchored
conditional contrast is taken to be affine, $\tau(\mathbf{x})=\alpha+\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\mathbf{x}$,
with $\boldsymbol{\beta}=(0.1,\;2,\;0.5)$, so that $S\boldsymbol{\beta}=(1,1,2)$ and
$\|S\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2=\sqrt6$. By @thm-distance-linear-bias-bound the exact transport bias is
$B_j=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\delta}_j=(S\boldsymbol{\beta})^\top\mathbf{z}_j=z_{j1}+z_{j2}+
2z_{j3}$:
$$
B_A=1.8,\qquad B_D=3.2,\qquad B_B=3.6,\qquad B_C=4.0 .
$$
The exact-bias ranking $A\prec D\prec B\prec C$ coincides with the standardized Euclidean and mean-SMD
rankings, and the standardized winner $A$ is indeed the minimum-bias comparator. The raw Euclidean winner
$C$ has the **largest** bias of the four, $4.0$; selecting by raw distance would have chosen the worst
comparator, the concrete reversal promised by @prp-distance-scale-dependence. The Mahalanobis winner $D$
has bias $3.2$, larger than $A$'s: $D$'s gap points exactly in the worst-case direction
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta}$ for this $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ (shown below), so its bias attains its
Mahalanobis bound, while $A$'s bias is far below its own.

The Cauchy-Schwarz bounds and their equality cases are worth seeing. The standardized bound
$\|S\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2\,d_{SE}=\sqrt6\,d_{SE}$ gives, for Study $B$,
$$
\sqrt6\cdot\sqrt{2.16}=\sqrt{12.96}=3.600=|B_B|,
$$
an exact equality, because $\mathbf{z}_B=(0.6,0.6,1.2)=0.6\,(1,1,2)=0.6\,S\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is parallel
to $S\boldsymbol{\beta}$, meeting the equality condition of @eq-distance-bias-se. The Mahalanobis bound
$\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\,d_M=\sqrt{8}\,d_M$ gives, for Study $D$,
$$
\sqrt8\cdot\sqrt{1.28}=\sqrt{10.24}=3.200=|B_D|,
$$
again exact, because $\boldsymbol{\delta}_D=(8,0.2,4)=0.4\,(20,0.5,10)=0.4\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is parallel to $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta}$, meeting the equality condition
of @eq-distance-bias-mah (one verifies $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta}=(20,0.5,10)$ and
$\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta}=8$). For every study both bounds dominate the
exact bias, as they must. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reading the four rankings, and where $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ comes from.** The calculation compresses into
one interpretation table.

| Criterion | Winner | Why it wins | What an HTA analyst should conclude |
|:--|:--:|:--|:--|
| Raw Euclidean $d_E$ | $C$ | dominated by age, the covariate with the largest numerical scale, on which $C$ is closest | discard: the choice is an artifact of units (@prp-distance-scale-dependence) |
| Standardized Euclidean $d_{SE}$ | $A$ | smallest gap in standard-deviation units, equal weight per covariate | defensible default; here it also happens to be the minimum-bias choice |
| Mahalanobis $d_M$ | $D$ | $D$'s age-biomarker move follows the index correlation, so it is "cheap" | defensible when the correlation is trusted, but here *not* the minimum-bias choice |
| Exact bias ($\boldsymbol{\beta}$ known) | $A$ | smallest $|\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\delta}_j|$ | the truth for *this* $\boldsymbol{\beta}$, which is unknown at selection time |

: Why each criterion selects a different comparator, and how to report the disagreement. {#tbl-distance-interpretation}

The vector $\boldsymbol{\beta}=(0.1,2,0.5)$ is a **sensitivity input**, not a quantity available when the
comparator is chosen. In practice it would be borrowed from a published regression of the outcome on the
covariates, elicited from clinical experts, or, most honestly, varied across a plausible range with the
ranking recomputed at each setting; here it is a teaching device that lets us see, after the fact, which
distance happened to align with the truth. Because it is unknown up front, the practical recommendation is
the one the table's last two columns dramatize: report the ranking under several distances, flag any
disagreement as a signal that the choice is geometry-dependent, and carry the ambiguity into the
sensitivity analysis rather than trusting a single number. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The lesson of the example.** Three reputable distances selected three different comparators. Standardized
Euclidean distance happened to rank by the true bias here because its implicit geometry, equal weight per
standardized covariate, was closer to the contrast direction $S\boldsymbol{\beta}=(1,1,2)$ than the
Mahalanobis geometry was. For other $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ the verdict can differ: by the equality cases of
@thm-distance-linear-bias-bound, $d_{SE}$ ranks candidates by their worst-case bias over all
$\boldsymbol{\beta}$ with $\|S\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2\le1$, and $d_M$ over all $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ with
$\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta}\le1$. Since $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is unknown at selection time, no distance is guaranteed to rank by bias; this is
@prp-distance-diagnostic-not-validity made arithmetic. The defensible practice is to report the ranking
under several distances, flag disagreement as a signal that the choice is geometry-dependent, and carry the
ambiguity into the sensitivity analysis rather than trusting a single number. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Connection to the Coq formalization {#sec-distance-coq}

Aggregate-level distance matching is a **design heuristic**, a rule for choosing which comparator to adjust
toward, and unlike the estimators of Parts IV and V it makes no claim of unbiasedness that a proof
assistant could certify. Its absence from the companion Coq development is therefore deliberate, not an
item left on a backlog: there is no `theories/DistanceMatching.v` because there is no correctness theorem
about the *selection rule* itself to mechanize. What the chapter does prove is elementary linear algebra
and analysis, and every piece already lives in the development in another guise. The whitening identity
@eq-distance-whitening is a one-line consequence of $(BB^\top)^{-1}=B^{-\top}B^{-1}$ and the existence of a
matrix square root, the latter being the symmetric-square-root construction underlying @thm-cov-psd. The
linear bias bounds @eq-distance-bias-se and @eq-distance-bias-mah are the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, the
same inequality the development formalizes for the effective-sample-size bound: the machine-checked
`Theorem ESS_upper_bound` of `theories/MAIC.v` (tagged on @thm-maic-ess-bound) is built from the
elementary $2xy\le x^2+y^2$ assembled by induction into a Cauchy-Schwarz statement, and a future
`DistanceMatching.v` could reuse that lemma verbatim to certify @thm-distance-linear-bias-bound.
Schematically, the single statement such a file would prove is one Cauchy-Schwarz application,

```coq
(* Linear bias bound, schematic form of Theorem distance-linear-bias-bound. *)
(* |beta . delta| <= ||beta||_Sigma * ||delta||_{inverse Sigma}. *)
Theorem distance_linear_bias_bound :
  forall (Sigma : SPDMatrix) (beta delta : Vector),
    Rabs (dot beta delta)
      <= sqrt (quad_form Sigma beta) * sqrt (quad_form (inverse Sigma) delta).
```

which is exactly @eq-distance-bias-mah, the Mahalanobis factor
$\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_j\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}}$ written out. The
non-identification proposition @prp-distance-diagnostic-not-validity is a pair of finite arithmetic
counterexamples and would formalize directly. None of these results is currently mechanized, so this
chapter carries no `[machine-checked]` tags; Chapter 30 documents the boundary of the formal development,
of which distance matching lies outside.

## Notes and references {#sec-distance-notes}

Aggregate-level covariate-distance matching is an extension beyond the population-adjustment theory of
@phillippo2019thesis, motivated by the disconnected-network and single-arm settings that the multilevel
unanchored meta-regression of @chandler2025mlumr addresses and that the transportability reframing of
@chandler2026transport places in estimand terms. The practical rule of selecting the candidate study
minimizing a covariate-summary distance is described in the Bristol Compass blog on extending ML-NMR to
disconnected networks [@perren2024compass], and the suite of distances studied here, standardized Euclidean
(the default), Euclidean, Mahalanobis, Manhattan, Minkowski, Gower, and mean-absolute
standardized-mean-difference, is the diagnostic toolkit implemented in the `uitc` R package [@uitc].

The distances themselves are classical. The Mahalanobis distance and its whitening interpretation
(@thm-mahalanobis-whitening) originate with @mahalanobis1936; its reduction to standardized Euclidean distance
for diagonal covariance and its full affine invariance (@thm-distance-scale-invariance) are standard facts
of multivariate analysis, here proved from @thm-cov-psd. The Gower distance for mixed continuous and
binary data is due to @gower1971. Minkowski's inequality, invoked in @prp-distance-metric-properties for the
general $\ell_q$ triangle inequality, is the standard named result; the orders $q\in\{1,2,\infty\}$ used in
this book are proved directly there from the coordinatewise triangle inequality and Cauchy-Schwarz. The
mean-SMD diagnostic and the $|z|>0.1$ rule of thumb are the covariate-balance conventions of the
propensity-score literature, transposed from the individual level to study summaries.

The bias theory is the chapter's own contribution to the catalogue. The linear bound
@thm-distance-linear-bias-bound is the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality applied to the affine specialization of
the unanchored transport bias of @thm-unanchored-paic-consistency, and it makes precise the sense in which
comparator selection bounds the residual bias that the consistency theorem assumes away. The Lipschitz
bound @thm-lipschitz-bias-bound is the elementary coupling side of Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality; @villani2009 is a
reference for the duality and for the Wasserstein distance. The lower bound @prp-distance-wasserstein-lower-bound, that the mean gap never
exceeds the Wasserstein distance, uses the vector Jensen inequality @thm-jensen and is what makes the
non-identification of @prp-distance-diagnostic-not-validity unavoidable rather than accidental: mean
distance is a floor on distributional distance, never a ceiling. The reader who wants the residual and
unmeasured-confounding part of the problem, which distance matching cannot touch, should continue to the
quantitative bias analysis of Chapter 28, where the E-value and tipping-point methods quantify exactly the
bias that a zero distance fails to rule out.

This chapter corresponds to results O.1 (the comparator-selection problem), O.2 (Euclidean and
standardized Euclidean distance), O.3 (the Mahalanobis whitening equivalence), O.4 (the Manhattan,
Minkowski, Gower, and mean-SMD distances), O.5 (scale dependence and invariance), O.6 (the linear and
Lipschitz bias bounds), and O.7 (the non-identification caveat) of the proof catalogue in
`proofs/O_distance_matching.md`, expanding each catalogue sketch into a complete proof and adding the
metric-property proposition @prp-distance-metric-properties and the Wasserstein lower bound
@prp-distance-wasserstein-lower-bound.

## Exercises {#sec-distance-exercises}

An exercise marked $\star$ has a full worked solution in Appendix F. The exercises are tagged by type;
start with the warm-ups, which need only arithmetic, before the computation, proof, and challenge problems.

::: {#exr-distance-warmup-compute}
**(Warm-up, computation) Two distances by hand.** The index study reports covariate means
$\bar{\mathbf{x}}_0=(50,\,20)$ on (age in years, biomarker in units) with reference scales $s=(10,\,5)$.
Two candidate comparators report $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_1=(58,\,24)$ and $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_2=(46,\,30)$.
(a) Compute the raw Euclidean and the standardized Euclidean distance of each candidate to the index, and
state which candidate each distance selects. (b) Using the index covariance
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}100&30\\30&25\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]$, compute the two
Mahalanobis distances and say whether they agree with the standardized ranking. You can check your method
against the fully worked @exm-distance-two-trials.
:::

::: {#exr-distance-warmup-memo}
**(Warm-up, interpretation) A comparator-selection memo.** Using @exm-distance-comparator-ranking, write a
short decision memo, one paragraph, for an HTA submission that (a) names the comparator you would carry
forward and why, (b) reports the disagreement among the raw, standardized, and Mahalanobis rankings and
explains it in one sentence a non-mathematician could follow, and (c) states what you would do if the
Mahalanobis winner (Study $D$) had poor clinical comparability, say a different line of therapy, while the
standardized winner (Study $A$) had better trial-design similarity. Which would you choose, and what does
@sec-distance-workflow say about the order in which comparability and distance are assessed?
:::

::: {#exr-distance-rescale-ranking}
**(Computation) Reference scale changes the winner.** Recompute the standardized Euclidean ranking in
@exm-distance-comparator-ranking using comparator-reported standard deviations $s'=(8,\,0.5,\,6)$ in place
of the index scales $s=(10,\,0.5,\,4)$. Report the new $d_{SE}$ for all four studies and the new winner,
and explain why @thm-distance-scale-invariance does **not** apply (the change is not a coherent rescaling
of a single coordinate system but a change of reference scales alone). Comment on which reference scale is
preferable when index IPD is available.
:::

::: {#exr-distance-chebyshev}
**(Computation) Worst-covariate selection.** For the four studies of @exm-distance-comparator-ranking compute the
Chebyshev distance $d_\infty=\max_\ell|z_{j\ell}|$ and the Minkowski distances $d_3$ and $d_4$. Show that
the ranking under $d_q$ moves toward the Chebyshev ranking as $q$ grows, and identify the study whose
selection is most sensitive to the choice of $q$. Interpret the result for a decision-maker who regards a
single badly mismatched covariate as disqualifying.
:::

::: {#exr-distance-minkowski-metric}
**(Proof) The triangle inequality at the boundary.** Prove that $d_q$ in @eq-distance-minkowski is a metric for
every $q\in[1,\infty]$ by establishing Minkowski's inequality $\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{w}\|_q\le
\|\mathbf{u}\|_q+\|\mathbf{w}\|_q$ from Hölder's inequality, and show by the explicit three-point
configuration of @prp-distance-metric-properties that the triangle inequality fails for every
$q\in(0,1)$. Conclude that the `uitc` restriction $q\ge1$ is exactly the range in which the Minkowski
"distance" deserves the name.
:::

::: {#exr-distance-affine-invariance}
**($\star$, proof) Full affine invariance of the Mahalanobis distance.** Prove that if the covariates are
reparameterized by any invertible affine map $\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{c}$ and the covariance
is transformed accordingly to $A\boldsymbol{\Sigma}A^\top$, then the Mahalanobis distance is unchanged,
whereas the standardized Euclidean distance is invariant only for diagonal $A$. Exhibit a nondiagonal
$2\times2$ invertible $A$ and a pair of candidates whose standardized Euclidean ranking is reversed by the
reparameterization while their Mahalanobis ranking is preserved. Explain what this says about the sense in
which Mahalanobis distance is the "coordinate-free" member of the family.
:::

::: {#exr-distance-secondmoment}
**($\star$, challenge) Matching means and variances is still not enough.** Strengthen
@prp-distance-diagnostic-not-validity by constructing two scalar covariate distributions with **identical
mean and identical variance**, hence zero distance under any diagnostic built from the first two moments,
whose target effects differ under a nonlinear contrast. (Hint: let $\mathcal{P}_0$ put mass $\tfrac12$ at
each of $\pm1$, and let $\mathcal{P}_1$ put mass $\tfrac34$ at $0$ and mass $\tfrac18$ at each of $\pm2$;
verify both have mean $0$ and variance $1$, then evaluate the quartic contrast $\tau(x)=x^4$.) Report the
two target effects, the resulting bias, and the implication for MAIC second-moment balancing: balancing
through any fixed finite set of moments leaves a residual bias for sufficiently nonlinear contrasts.
:::

::: {#exr-distance-wasserstein}
**(Computation) Verifying the Lipschitz bound.** For the two distributions of @prp-distance-diagnostic-not-validity Part
1, $\mathcal{P}_0=\delta_0$ and $\mathcal{P}_1=\tfrac12\delta_{-1}+\tfrac12\delta_{+1}$, compute the
Wasserstein-1 distance $W_\rho(\mathcal{P}_1,\mathcal{P}_0)$ under the Euclidean ground metric by
exhibiting the optimal coupling, confirm the mean-distance lower bound
$d_E=0\le W_\rho$ of @prp-distance-wasserstein-lower-bound, and verify the Lipschitz bias bound
@eq-distance-lipschitz for the contrast $\tau(x)=x^2$ on the support $\{-1,0,1\}$ with its Lipschitz
constant $L=2$. State why the bound is not tight here and which feature of $\tau$ would make it tight.
:::

::: {#exr-distance-ess-tradeoff}
**(Interpretation) Distance against effective sample size.** Argue that, all else equal, a comparator with a larger
standardized Euclidean distance from the index population requires more aggressive reweighting in a
subsequent unanchored MAIC and hence a lower effective sample size. Using @thm-maic-ess-bound and the
variance-inflation factor $n/\mathrm{ESS}$, explain why comparator selection trades bias (from any part of the gap
left unadjusted, bounded under @thm-distance-linear-bias-bound) against variance (from the part that is
matched, governed by the ESS), and sketch how this
trade-off would enter a mean-squared-error criterion for choosing among candidates of comparable distance.
Relate the trade-off to the simulation-study estimands of Chapter 29.
:::
